Highland Hidden Gems: Beyond the NC500

The NC500 has put the Scottish Highlands on every motorcyclist's bucket list. But the Highlands are vast, and the NC500 covers only a fraction of what's on offer. These ten hidden gems are the places that most riders miss — the secret roads, remote peninsulas, and overlooked regions that the locals want to keep quiet about.

1. Ardnamurchan Peninsula

The B8007 to Ardnamurchan Point is the most westerly point of the British mainland (not Land's End!). The single-track road winds through a landscape of volcanic rock, Atlantic views, and complete solitude. The lighthouse at the tip is magnificent. Access via the Corran Ferry from Fort William.

2. Knoydart

Britain's last wilderness — Knoydart has no road access. But the boat from Mallaig to Inverie is an adventure, and walking or cycling in this roadless peninsula is unforgettable. The Old Forge pub in Inverie claims to be Britain's most remote pub.

3. Glen Affric

Glen Affric is often called Scotland's most beautiful glen. The road from Cannich penetrates deep into ancient Caledonian pine forest with views of Loch Affric and surrounding Munros. The road ends at a car park, but the sense of entering a primordial landscape is powerful.

4. Strathnaver Trail

The B871 through Strathnaver in Sutherland passes through the landscape of the Highland Clearances — one of the most traumatic chapters in Scottish history. The Strathnaver Museum at Bettyhill tells the story of communities forcibly removed. The road itself is empty and atmospheric.

The Highlands reward curiosity. Every dead-end road leads somewhere extraordinary. Take the road less travelled — that's where the real Scotland lives.

5-7. Forgotten West Coast Peninsulas

  • Scoraig — Off-grid community on the north shore of Little Loch Broom, reachable only by boat or foot
  • Coigach — The minor road from Achiltibuie loops around a peninsula of extraordinary beauty with views to the Summer Isles
  • Sandwood Bay — Britain's most beautiful beach, reachable by a 4-mile walk from the road end at Blairmore

8. The Monadhliath Mountains

The Monadhliath range between the Cairngorms and the Great Glen is one of Scotland's least-visited mountain areas. The minor road from Laggan through Glen Banchor offers wild, empty riding with views across heather moorland to distant peaks.

9. The Black Isle

Despite its name, the Black Isle is a peninsula, not an island, just north of Inverness. Chanonry Point is one of the best places in Britain to see bottlenose dolphins. The quiet farming villages and woodland walks make a peaceful contrast to the dramatic Highlands.

10. Rannoch Moor

The A82 crosses Rannoch Moor between Glen Coe and Tyndrum, but the road to Rannoch Station from the B846 penetrates the heart of this vast, wild plateau. It's one of the most remote places in Britain — a landscape of peat bogs, lochs, and enormous sky.

Exploring Tips

Many of these hidden gems are on dead-end roads — you'll need to retrace your route. Fuel is scarce in remote areas, so always fill up before exploring. Mobile signal is non-existent in most of these locations. Carry supplies and let someone know your plans if heading to very remote areas. faq.q: Where is the most westerly point of mainland Britain?
faq.a: It is Ardnamurchan Point, not Land's End. The single-track B8007 winds out to the lighthouse through a landscape of volcanic rock, Atlantic views and complete solitude. Access is via the Corran Ferry from Fort William, a short crossing that opens up one of the Highlands' most rewarding and least-visited peninsulas.

faq.q: Which glen is worth the detour?
faq.a: Glen Affric is often called Scotland's most beautiful glen. The road from Cannich penetrates deep into ancient Caledonian pine forest with views of Loch Affric and surrounding Munros. It ends at a car park, but the sense of entering a primordial landscape is powerful. It is a dead-end, so you retrace your route.

faq.q: How should I prepare for these remote areas?
faq.a: Many of these gems are on dead-end roads, so you will need to retrace your route and budget extra time. Fuel is scarce, so always fill up before exploring. Mobile signal is non-existent in most of these locations, so carry supplies and let someone know your plans if heading somewhere very remote.

faq.q: Are any of these gems close to Inverness?
faq.a: Yes. The Black Isle, which is actually a peninsula, sits just north of Inverness. Chanonry Point is one of the best places in Britain to see bottlenose dolphins, and the quiet farming villages and woodland walks make a peaceful contrast to the more dramatic Highlands further west.

faq.q: Which of these can I reach without a boat?
faq.a: Most, including Ardnamurchan (via the Corran Ferry), Glen Affric, Coigach, the Strathnaver Trail, the Monadhliath and Rannoch Moor via the B846 to Rannoch Station. Knoydart is the exception, being Britain's last road-free wilderness, reached by boat from Mallaig to Inverie, home to the remote Old Forge pub.
